title: Kindness to those who don't fight you
hook: Allah doesn't forbid kindness and justice toward those who haven't fought you (60:8)
tomorrow: Why say what you don't do?

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ibrahim, firm in faith, tender with his father, quick to feed strangers. Your line was an excellent example. Today closes the week.

Asma', the daughter of Abu Bakr, is living in Medina when her mother arrives from Mecca. The mother hasn't become Muslim. Mecca is the city that drove the daughter's community out. One report says the mother came bearing gifts. Asma' doesn't know what to do. Should she let her in? Accept the gifts? Can she be kind to her own mother across this line? She goes to ask the Prophet ﷺ.
screen: `CAN SHE BE KIND ACROSS THE LINE?`

segments.voice: Bukhari and Muslim record his answer. Yes, he said: keep good ties with your mother. Some reports connect this verse to her story. Surah sixty, verse eight. Pickthall: "Allah forbiddeth you not those who warred not against you on account of religion and drove you not out from your homes, that ye should show them kindness and deal justly with them. Lo! Allah loveth the just dealers." Two words do the work. The first is tabarruhum, show them kindness, from the root b-r-r, the same root as birr, the word the Qur'an and hadith use for kindness to parents. The second is tuqsitu, deal justly, from qist, fairness. And the verse ends with God's love for the muqsitin, the people of fairness. So this isn't permission for a cold politeness. It uses family words. People of another faith who live in peace with the community may be shown birr and qist: warmth and fairness. The surah came in a hard time, when the community was in conflict with Mecca, and the next verse draws a line around those who actually fought them and drove them out. Scholars have discussed how the two verses fit together across history. But the core of verse eight is plain: kindness and fairness are not forbidden, and fairness is loved. A mother at the door, not a Muslim. The answer: yes, be good to her.
screen: `ASMA' AND HER MOTHER.` · `TABARRUHUM: SHOW THEM BIRR.` · `QIST: DEAL JUSTLY.` · `GOD LOVES THE PEOPLE OF FAIRNESS.`

segments.voice: Think of someone whose faith, or lack of one, is different from yours: a neighbor, a coworker, a relative, a friend. Picture their face, and breathe in warmth toward them, breathe out fairness. Then choose one small, concrete kindness, a message, a favor, a genuine question about their week, and hold it until it feels doable.
Birr: kindness, the root behind God's permission in Surah Al-Mumtahanah to be warm and fair with those who haven't fought you over faith. Today's word.
Your line: kindness and justice to all. The week ran from deeds sent ahead, through the humbled mountain and the beautiful names, to Ibrahim and Asma' at her door. A full week, done.

howItsDone: Muslim scholars cite 60:8 in teaching good relations with neighbors of other faiths, and the story of Asma' bint Abi Bakr and her mother is often told to show that family ties continue across differences of belief.

Only to people of your own faith; the verse is about fellow believers.
